name: Lip plumper (capsaicin)

lead: Capsaicin lip plumpers are glosses or balms containing a chili-derived irritant, sometimes with menthol, cinnamon, peppermint or ginger. They produce a tingle or burn and a short-lived swelling that makes lips look fuller within minutes. They are positioned as a needle-free alternative to filler.

Capsaicin activates heat-sensitive receptors on sensory nerves and is described as increasing blood flow and causing mild swelling, with effects reported to last from minutes to a few hours. A separate class of hydration-based plumpers uses humectants such as hyaluronic acid and does not aim to irritate. Published evidence is limited to small, mostly open-label studies of branded products.

paras: It is applied like a regular lip gloss or balm, often before makeup or a night out, and reapplied when the effect fades. Many products combine several active ingredients.

Case reports and reviews document contact urticaria and allergic contact reactions to lip cosmetics, including plumpers. Grokipedia reports that frequent use of irritant formulas may cause dryness and sensitivity.

angle.text: A chili-based gloss, sometimes with menthol or cinnamon, irritates the lips so they swell briefly and look fuller, a non-injectable option. The swelling is visible within minutes and fades in minutes to a few hours. Published studies are small and mostly open-label.

lead: A capsaicin lip plumper is a topical cosmetic applied to the lips that uses an irritant, most often capsaicin from chili peppers, sometimes with menthol, cinnamon, peppermint or ginger, to produce a brief tingling or burning sensation and temporary swelling that makes the lips look fuller.[1] It is marketed as a non-injectable alternative to lip filler.[1]

Irritant formulas are described as working by stimulating nerve endings and increasing local blood flow, with effects reported to last from minutes to a few hours.[1] A separate class of "hydration-based" plumpers relies on humectants such as hyaluronic acid and does not aim to irritate.[1]

Published evidence is limited to small, mostly open-label studies of proprietary products, many of which combine several ingredients. Case reports and reviews document contact urticaria and allergic contact reactions to lip cosmetics, including plumpers.[2][3][4]
infobox: Capsaicin, often with menthol, cinnamon, ginger or peppermint
Minutes to a few hours (per Grokipedia)[1]

paras: Irritant-based plumpers apply a mild irritant to the lips so that the skin reddens and swells slightly, which is perceived as added volume.[1] Users commonly describe a tingling, warming or stinging sensation that products treat as a sign the formula is active.[1]

Capsaicin acts on heat-sensitive receptors on sensory nerves, which is why it feels hot; the same activation is described as driving vasodilation and mild inflammation.[1] Hydration-based products use ingredients such as hyaluronic acid, glycerin and peptides and are described as giving a smoother, subtler effect.[1]

Grokipedia credits DuWop Cosmetics' Lip Venom, launched in 1999, with introducing the first topical plumper, and describes the category growing through the 2000s before a shift toward tingle-free, hydration-based formulas and a renewed interest in the late 2010s.[1] This history comes from a single AI-generated source.

Evidence is limited. A four-week open-label study of a two-step lip treatment that included a niacin-based plumper reported on moisturization and fullness, but it tested a combined regimen rather than capsaicin alone.[5] A 2018 open-label trial in the Journal of Drugs in Dermatology evaluated the duration, efficacy and safety of a novel plumper,[6] and a 2017 study in the International Journal of Cosmetic Science asked how long the volumizing effect of a ginger-based plumper lasts.[7] Grokipedia summarises the literature as showing short-lived volume with small, unblinded studies.[1]

A 2009 case report in the Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology described contact urticaria from a lip plumper in a young boy and discussed the mechanisms and the social reasons for use.[3] A 2016 review catalogued cosmetic ingredients that cause immediate-type contact reactions,[2] and a 2024 systematic review examined allergic contact dermatitis to lip-care products.[4]
Grokipedia reports that frequent use of irritant formulas may cause dryness, scaling, increased sensitivity or allergic reactions, and that experts suggest caution for people with sensitive lips.[1]

The studies available are small and mostly open-label, and they commonly test proprietary multi-ingredient products rather than capsaicin alone.[5][6][7] No large randomized trial of a capsaicin-only lip plumper was identified.

timeline.event: DuWop Lip Venom is launched and credited with starting the category (per Grokipedia).[1]
